ABSTRACT
Hybrid technologies are considered one of the key solutions for CO2 reduction in large
off-highway machines that operate for long hours in suburban areas with limited access to energy refueling
infrastructure. The effectiveness of CO2 reduction through hybridization largely depends on the hybrid
powertrain architecture and its operating strategies. This paper uses a parallel-series hybrid wheel loader
as a research platform to investigate and optimize energy management strategies. The parallel-series
hybrid powertrain consists of a pure electric propulsion system and a parallel hybrid working hydraulic
system. In this paper, a real-time capable energy management strategy based on an optimization theory is
presented. This strategy combines Dynamic Programming (DP) and Pontryagin’s Minimum Principle (PMP)
to optimize both engine start-stop sequence and torque split between the engine and the electric machine,
while balancing the disadvantages of each control theory. To enable real-time implementation of the proposed
control strategy, short-term vehicle power demand is predicted using a state detection algorithm developed
to account for the repetitive nature of the duty cycles of a wheel loader. Simulation results indicate that
fuel consumption can be reduced by 4.0% compared to a rule-based strategy in a typical loading cycle. Test
results with a prototype hybrid wheel loader conﬁrm that the proposed control strategy operates in real-time
and improves system efﬁciency. In particular, the average engine brake fuel consumption (BSFC) improved
by 0.7% in the loading cycle and by 1.3% in a more realistic mission cycle that combines the loading cycle
with driving.

classiﬁcation of energy management strategies developed for
off-highway machines can be found in [6] and [7]. A primary
distinction is made between rule-based and optimization-
based control strategies.
In rule-based control strategies, control decisions are made
based on predeﬁned rules derived from prior knowledge of
the system, operating conditions, and empirical experience.
These strategies are often preferred for real-world vehicle
implementation because of their low computational effort.
For this reason, existing hybrid construction machines pri-
marily adopt rule-based strategies [6], and extensive research
has been conducted in this area. In [8], a rule-based strategy
was developed for an excavator equipped with a parallel
hybrid system for the hydraulic pump and an electric swing
motor. This strategy adjusts the motor-generator power based
on the required pump power. Similarly, in [9], various rule-
based control strategies were designed for a parallel hybrid
wheel loader. These strategies were evaluated in simulations
in terms of fuel efﬁciency and achieved a 3–13% reduction in
fuel consumption compared to a conventional wheel loader.
Rule-based control strategies have also been validated in
real-world operations. In [10], a prototype hybrid excavator
with a parallel hybrid system for the pump and an electric
swing motor was developed. A rule-based control strategy
was implemented and tested in this prototype excavator.
Rule-based strategies are simple and have a low compu-
tational effort. However, they are typically optimized for a
speciﬁc mission cycle and do not guarantee the same level of
performance in real-world cycles.
In contrast, optimization-based strategies introduce control
objectives by deﬁning cost functions to be optimized and
thus providing proof of optimality. Dynamic Programming
(DP) [11] is one of the most widely used techniques for
global optimization. However, DP requires prior knowledge
of the entire cycle, and its high computational burden makes
real-time energy management highly challenging. In [12],
a rule-based control strategy for a hybrid excavator was
developed by analyzing the results of a DP-based control
strategy. Furthermore, DP is also used as a benchmark
strategy [13], [14].
Control strategies based on Pontryagin’s Minimum Princi-
ple (PMP) are strong candidates for real-time capable control
strategies. The application of the Equivalent Consump-
tion Minimization Strategy (ECMS) to off-highway hybrid
machines has been widely documented in the literature [13],
[14], [15]. In [13], an ECMS-based energy management strat-
egy was implemented in a hybrid excavator equipped with an
electric swing motor. Test results with the real vehicle demon-
strated approximately 30% reduction in fuel consumption
compared to a conventional excavator. PMP-based strategies
require lower computational effort but cannot handle discrete
states, such as mode transitions and gear shifts, within their
control framework. To address this limitation, the authors
of [16] combined DP and PMP to derive the optimal start-
stop sequence of the internal combustion engine (ICE) for
plug-in electric vehicles. Their simulations conﬁrmed that the

DP-PMP algorithm yields near-optimal performance. Other
studies [17], [18], [19] extended this approach to optimize
both ICE start-stop and gear shifting for on-highway hybrid
vehicles. However, to the best of the authors’ knowledge,
DP-PMP-based energy management strategies have not yet
been validated through real-world testing. Furthermore, their
application is limited to on-highway vehicles so far. In this
paper, we propose a DP-PMP-based control algorithm as a
real-time energy management strategy for a hybrid wheel
loader. The main contributions of this paper are as follows:
• We adapt the DP-PMP approach to off-highway hybrid
powertrains and formulate an energy management
algorithm.
• We present the control architecture, including support
functions, to ensure real-time implementation of the
developed algorithm.
• We evaluate control performance in terms of fuel con-
sumption in both simulation and real-world testing.
Additionally, we assess the real-time capability of the
controller.
The rest of this paper is structured as follows: Section II

presents the developed hybrid powertrain and the investigated
mission cycles. Section III describes the modeling of key
powertrain components for the implementation of an optimal
control strategy. Section IV details the adopted optimal con-
trol algorithm, the controller design, and its implementation
in the prototype hybrid wheel loader. The developed con-
trol algorithm is evaluated through simulations in Section V
and validated via real-world testing in Section VI. Finally,
Section VII concludes the paper.

2) WORKING HYDRAULIC SYSTEM
A hydraulic pump with ﬁxed displacement driven by the ICE
provides hydraulic oil ﬂow to the valve system. There are
four cylinders in the hydraulic system, namely two steering
cylinders, one tilt cylinder and one lift cylinder. The lift
and tilt cylinders enable a wide range of work with various
attachments. The most typical attachment is a bucket used for
moving gravel, rocks, and other materials, but other attach-
ments such as forklift, timber grapple, snowplow, sweeper
roller and material handling arm are also used for special
purposes [20]. The steering system is a so-called articulated
steering system. The relative yaw angle between the front and
rear part of the vehicle is changed by two hydraulic cylinders,
allowing the vehicle to be signiﬁcantly more maneuverable
than a vehicle with coordinated steering [21], [22]. The steer-
ing wheel column is connected to the orbitrol, which supplies
oil proportional to the amount of steering wheel rotation to the
steering cylinders in the desired direction. The priority valve
supplies the required oil to the steering cylinders ﬁrst, giving
priority to steering for safety reasons. The remaining oil is
supplied to the open center control valve, where the direction
and ﬂow rate are controlled by the spools.

3) PROPULSION SYSTEM
A hydraulic pump with variable displacement driven by the
ICE forms a hydrostatic transmission (HST) together with a
variable displacement hydraulic motor. All four wheels are
mechanically connected to the output shaft of the hydraulic
motor, enabling all-wheel drive functionality. There is a
hydraulically actuated two-speed transmission between the
HST output shaft and the cardan shaft. With the second gear,
high-speed driving up to 36 km/h is possible.
B. MISSION CYCLES

Wheel loaders cover a wide range of work, and their appli-
cations are versatile. Among others, the most common and
widely studied [23], [24], [25] wheel loader cycle is a loading
cycle, also called a V-cycle because of the shape of the
vehicle movement. Fig. 2 presents a schematic top view
of the V-cycle, while the top two subplots in Fig. 3 show
the measured vehicle speed and cylinder stroke during the
V-cycle. In this cycle, a wheel loader loads materials such as
soil, gravel and sand into a load receiver, which is typically
a truck placed next to a pile of material. The V-cycle can be
divided into four parts. In phase A, the wheel loader moves
forward to a pile of material and ﬁlls the bucket with material.
In phase B, the vehicle drives backwards and returns to the
starting point. In this phase, the bucket’s position remains

almost unchanged. In phase C, the vehicle steers slightly
and moves forward towards the load receiver. While driving
forward, the bucket is raised by extending the lift cylinder.
After stopping the vehicle in front of the load receiver, the tilt
cylinder is extended to empty the bucket. Finally, in phase
D, the vehicle reverses and returns to the starting point.
The bucket is lowered by contracting the lift cylinder while
driving backwards. The series of phase A to D is repeated
several times until the load receiver is full of material.
FIGURE 2. Schematic top view of the V-cycle.

The bottom two subplots in Fig. 3 compare the requested
hydraulic ﬂow rate with the actual supply from the hydraulic
pump. There is a large gap between the supplied ﬂow rate
and the requested ﬂow rate, especially during phase A and
phase B, as marked by red arrows in Fig. 3.
In these phases, the bucket is moved only slightly, resulting
in a low requested ﬂow rate. However, since the hydraulic
pump is connected to the same ICE output shaft as the HST,
it is driven at high speeds when the operator presses the accel-
erator pedal to drive the vehicle. As a result, the hydraulic
pump generates an unnecessarily large amount of oil ﬂow
within the hydraulic system, which returns to the tank without
doing useful hydraulic work. The key to reducing hydraulic
losses from the operational perspective is, therefore, to keep
the pump speed as close as possible to the speed required for
the requested hydraulic ﬂow rate.
Another mission cycle considered in this paper is a combi-
nation of the V-cycle with short driving, as shown in Fig. 4.
This combined cycle serves as a more realistic mission cycle
in a quarry. After ﬁve repetitions of the V-cycle (marked as
1 in Fig. 4), the wheel loader transports material to another
location to increase productivity instead of simply waiting for
another truck to arrive at the loading area. First, the bucket
is loaded (2 in Fig. 4), and then the vehicle drives with a
full bucket (3 in Fig. 4). After transportation, the bucket
is emptied (4 in Fig. 4), and then the vehicle drives the
same route with an empty bucket (5 in Fig. 4) to return to

C. PARALLEL-SERIES HYBRID SYSTEM

The powertrain of the baseline wheel loader shown in Fig. 1
has been converted to a parallel-series hybrid system. Fig. 5
shows the schematic of the developed parallel-series hybrid
system for a wheel loader.
The parallel-series hybrid combines aspects of both par-

allel and series topologies. In this conﬁguration, the ICE is
not directly connected to the drivetrain, allowing independent
control of the ICE regardless of the drivetrain speed. The
hydraulic pump is driven by the P2 parallel hybrid system
consisting of an electric machine (P2 EM) and a downsized
ICE. Pure electric operation is possible with the clutch located
between the P2 EM and the ICE.
The hydraulic drivetrain has been electriﬁed with two elec-

tric machines, integrated into each axle. In general, hydraulic
motors have higher torque density compared to electric
motors [26]. A reduction transmission is integrated into each
electric drive unit (EDU) to fulﬁll the maximum vehicle
speed target and the high torque demand at low vehicle
speeds. Details and technical data of the hybrid system are
summarized in Table 1.

D. OPERATOR INTERFACE AND OPERATING STRATEGIES

FOR PARALLEL-SERIES HYBRID SYSTEM
In the conventional wheel loader, the operator presses the
accelerator pedal to regulate the ICE speed to get the desired
hydraulic ﬂow rate from the pump or to get the desired
propulsion torque. This brings with it several drawbacks, and
the operator interface and operating strategies for the hybrid
wheel loader must be designed to overcome them. These are:
1) Low efﬁciency in the working hydraulic system: Since

the hydraulic pump is coupled with the drivetrain via
ICE, the pump runs at high speeds e.g. during vehicle
acceleration even though the hydraulic oil required for
steering is quite low, causing large losses due to excess
ﬂow.
2) High operator workload: As the ICE drives both work-

ing hydraulic pumps, the accelerator pedal position
inﬂuences the pump ﬂow rate and the propulsion
torque. This means that the values controlled by the
operator – cylinder speed and vehicle acceleration –
must be adjusted via additional inputs, namely the joy-
stick and brake pedal.
Fig. 7. shows the new operator interface developed for

the parallel-series hybrid wheel loader. Unlike conventional
wheel loaders, all operator inputs are forwarded to the Hybrid
Control Unit (HCU), which determines the target pump speed
and propulsion torque.
Since the propulsion system is decoupled from the working

hydraulic system, the accelerator pedal position is solely used
to determine the propulsion torque. The electriﬁed propulsion
system also offers the possibility of recuperating the kinetic
energy of the vehicle, which in conventional vehicles would
be lost as heat through mechanical brakes, through regenera-
tive braking. By calibrating the target propulsion to a negative

C. PARALLEL-SERIES HYBRID SYSTEM
The powertrain of the baseline wheel loader shown in Fig. 1
has been converted to a parallel-series hybrid system. Fig. 5
shows the schematic of the developed parallel-series hybrid
system for a wheel loader.
The parallel-series hybrid combines aspects of both par-
allel and series topologies. In this conﬁguration, the ICE is
not directly connected to the drivetrain, allowing independent
control of the ICE regardless of the drivetrain speed. The
hydraulic pump is driven by the P2 parallel hybrid system
consisting of an electric machine (P2 EM) and a downsized
ICE. Pure electric operation is possible with the clutch located
between the P2 EM and the ICE.
The hydraulic drivetrain has been electriﬁed with two elec-
tric machines, integrated into each axle. In general, hydraulic
motors have higher torque density compared to electric
motors [26]. A reduction transmission is integrated into each
electric drive unit (EDU) to fulﬁll the maximum vehicle
speed target and the high torque demand at low vehicle
speeds. Details and technical data of the hybrid system are

D. OPERATOR INTERFACE AND OPERATING STRATEGIES
FOR PARALLEL-SERIES HYBRID SYSTEM
In the conventional wheel loader, the operator presses the
accelerator pedal to regulate the ICE speed to get the desired
hydraulic ﬂow rate from the pump or to get the desired
propulsion torque. This brings with it several drawbacks, and
the operator interface and operating strategies for the hybrid
wheel loader must be designed to overcome them. These are:
1) Low efﬁciency in the working hydraulic system: Since
the hydraulic pump is coupled with the drivetrain via
ICE, the pump runs at high speeds e.g. during vehicle
acceleration even though the hydraulic oil required for
steering is quite low, causing large losses due to excess
ﬂow.
2) High operator workload: As the ICE drives both work-
ing hydraulic pumps, the accelerator pedal position
inﬂuences the pump ﬂow rate and the propulsion
torque. This means that the values controlled by the
operator – cylinder speed and vehicle acceleration –
must be adjusted via additional inputs, namely the joy-
stick and brake pedal.
Fig. 7. shows the new operator interface developed for
the parallel-series hybrid wheel loader. Unlike conventional
wheel loaders, all operator inputs are forwarded to the Hybrid
Control Unit (HCU), which determines the target pump speed
and propulsion torque.
Since the propulsion system is decoupled from the working
hydraulic system, the accelerator pedal position is solely used
to determine the propulsion torque. The electriﬁed propulsion
system also offers the possibility of recuperating the kinetic
energy of the vehicle, which in conventional vehicles would
be lost as heat through mechanical brakes, through regenera-
tive braking. By calibrating the target propulsion to a negative
value at a low pedal position, the operator can decelerate
the vehicle by releasing the accelerator pedal. In addition

B. CONTROLLER DESIGN AND IMPLEMENTATION OF THE

DP-PMP-BASED OPTIMAL ENERGY MANAGEMENT
STRATEGY
The optimization algorithm based on DP-PMP requires future
cycle information, such as the pump ﬂow rate, pressure, and
EDU power.
Compared to on-highway vehicles, predicting future power

demands of off-highway vehicles is more complicated, as it
depends not only on the speed proﬁle but also on factors
such as the interaction of the power take-offs (PTOs) with
the boundary conditions. One feature of off-highway mission

VII. CONCLUSION

This paper has presented a novel real-time capable energy
management strategy based on the DP-PMP algorithm for
a hybrid wheel loader. To enable real-time implementation,
wheel loader mission cycles were divided into small seg-
ments, and a future power demand prediction algorithm based
on the repetitiveness of the mission cycles was introduced.
Additionally, the timing of the ICE start-stop control decision
was changed from the conventional time-based approach to
machine state changes in order to further reduce the compu-
tational effort and to avoid unnecessary ICE start-stop events.
The developed energy management algorithm was tested

in a simulation environment, and the simulation results
conﬁrmed that the proposed strategy can reduce fuel con-
sumption by 3.3% in the V-cycle and 4.0% in the combined
cycle.
A detailed analysis of the powertrain energy ﬂow has

shown that the optimization-based control strategy reduces
losses in the hydraulic system by reducing the pump speed
in electric mode and uses the ICE more efﬁciently in areas
with lower BSFC. The test results with the demonstrator con-
ﬁrmed that the required time for the optimization calculation
is 2.2 seconds on the MABX II, proving that the proposed
strategy is capable of real-time operation. The test results with
the hybrid wheel loader conﬁrmed that the presented control
strategy can improve the BSFC of the ICE in both the V-cycle
and the combined cycle by using the ICE in areas with higher
efﬁciency. However, due to the varying workloads during
testing, it is difﬁcult to evaluate the overall fuel consumption
beneﬁts.
The proposed approach relies on correct state detection

to trigger optimization based on predicted power demand.
In practical implementation, when state detection conﬁdence
is insufﬁcient or misclassiﬁcation is detected, the controller
intentionally disables the DP–PMP optimization and falls
back to a conservative baseline strategy, such as a rule-
based controller or adaptive ECMS. This fallback mechanism
ensures robust and safe operation under uncertain or unfore-
seen conditions, while preserving the beneﬁts of optimization
when reliable predictions are available.
Future research could focus on analyzing the potential

for reducing raw pollutant emissions through reduced tran-
sient ICE operation, thanks to hybridization. Furthermore, the
integration of emission control into the optimization control
framework to investigate the optimal concept for exhaust
aftertreatment systems is another area for future studies.
In addition, the provision of future scenarios through the
networking of machines and their management as a ﬂeet on
the construction site is another research focus.

sections.heading: I. INTRODUCTION
sections.content:
The global concern over climate change is pushing automo-
tive manufacturers to reduce pollutant emissions from their
products. Since pollutant emission limits for the off-highway
sector have become more stringent, following the trend of
on-highway vehicles, it is expected that even stricter emis-
sion standards will be introduced in the off-highway sector.
Although greenhouse gases (GHG) emissions from the off-
highway sector are estimated to account for only 2% of the

The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and

approving it for publication was Md. Abdur Razzaque
.

total EU27 GHG emissions [1], reducing CO2 emissions in
this sector will have even greater signiﬁcance in the future,
as food production and construction demands are expected to
rise with the growing world population.
In this context, hybrid technologies have been attract-
ing the attention of researchers and construction machinery
manufacturers due to their onboard energy capacity and
ease of refueling [31]. Several hybrid construction machines
have already been developed in the past [2], [3], [4], [5].
The effectiveness of CO2 reduction through hybridization
depends not only on the hybrid powertrain architecture, but
also on its energy management strategies. An overview and

Y. Kakichi et al.: Real-Time Capable Optimal Energy Management Strategy for a Hybrid Wheel Loader

classiﬁcation of energy management strategies developed for
off-highway machines can be found in [6] and [7]. A primary
distinction is made between rule-based and optimization-
based control strategies.
In rule-based control strategies, control decisions are made
based on predeﬁned rules derived from prior knowledge of
the system, operating conditions, and empirical experience.
These strategies are often preferred for real-world vehicle
implementation because of their low computational effort.
For this reason, existing hybrid construction machines pri-
marily adopt rule-based strategies [6], and extensive research
has been conducted in this area. In [8], a rule-based strategy
was developed for an excavator equipped with a parallel
hybrid system for the hydraulic pump and an electric swing
motor. This strategy adjusts the motor-generator power based
on the required pump power. Similarly, in [9], various rule-
based control strategies were designed for a parallel hybrid
wheel loader. These strategies were evaluated in simulations
in terms of fuel efﬁciency and achieved a 3–13% reduction in
fuel consumption compared to a conventional wheel loader.
Rule-based control strategies have also been validated in
real-world operations. In [10], a prototype hybrid excavator
with a parallel hybrid system for the pump and an electric
swing motor was developed. A rule-based control strategy
was implemented and tested in this prototype excavator.
Rule-based strategies are simple and have a low compu-
tational effort. However, they are typically optimized for a
speciﬁc mission cycle and do not guarantee the same level of
performance in real-world cycles.
In contrast, optimization-based strategies introduce control
objectives by deﬁning cost functions to be optimized and
thus providing proof of optimality. Dynamic Programming
(DP) [11] is one of the most widely used techniques for
global optimization. However, DP requires prior knowledge
of the entire cycle, and its high computational burden makes
real-time energy management highly challenging. In [12],
a rule-based control strategy for a hybrid excavator was
developed by analyzing the results of a DP-based control
strategy. Furthermore, DP is also used as a benchmark
strategy [13], [14].
Control strategies based on Pontryagin’s Minimum Princi-
ple (PMP) are strong candidates for real-time capable control
strategies. The application of the Equivalent Consump-
tion Minimization Strategy (ECMS) to off-highway hybrid
machines has been widely documented in the literature [13],
[14], [15]. In [13], an ECMS-based energy management strat-
egy was implemented in a hybrid excavator equipped with an
electric swing motor. Test results with the real vehicle demon-
strated approximately 30% reduction in fuel consumption
compared to a conventional excavator. PMP-based strategies
require lower computational effort but cannot handle discrete
states, such as mode transitions and gear shifts, within their
control framework. To address this limitation, the authors
of [16] combined DP and PMP to derive the optimal start-
stop sequence of the internal combustion engine (ICE) for
plug-in electric vehicles. Their simulations conﬁrmed that the

2

DP-PMP algorithm yields near-optimal performance. Other
studies [17], [18], [19] extended this approach to optimize
both ICE start-stop and gear shifting for on-highway hybrid
vehicles. However, to the best of the authors’ knowledge,
DP-PMP-based energy management strategies have not yet
been validated through real-world testing. Furthermore, their
application is limited to on-highway vehicles so far. In this
paper, we propose a DP-PMP-based control algorithm as a
real-time energy management strategy for a hybrid wheel
loader. The main contributions of this paper are as follows:
• We adapt the DP-PMP approach to off-highway hybrid
powertrains and formulate an energy management
algorithm.
• We present the control architecture, including support
functions, to ensure real-time implementation of the
developed algorithm.
• We evaluate control performance in terms of fuel con-
sumption in both simulation and real-world testing.
Additionally, we assess the real-time capability of the
controller.
The rest of this paper is structured as follows: Section II

presents the developed hybrid powertrain and the investigated
mission cycles. Section III describes the modeling of key
powertrain components for the implementation of an optimal
control strategy. Section IV details the adopted optimal con-
trol algorithm, the controller design, and its implementation
in the prototype hybrid wheel loader. The developed con-
trol algorithm is evaluated through simulations in Section V
and validated via real-world testing in Section VI. Finally,
Section VII concludes the paper.

sections.heading: A. CONVENTIONAL POWERTRAIN
sections.content:
A conventional 7-ton class wheel loader depicted in Fig. 1
is used as a baseline for research. The powertrain of the
conventional wheel loader consists of three sub-systems:

1) POWER SOURCE
The baseline wheel loader is powered by a 3.6 L, 4-cylinder
Diesel internal combustion engine (ICE) with a maximum

Y. Kakichi et al.: Real-Time Capable Optimal Energy Management Strategy for a Hybrid Wheel Loader

power of 74.4 kW. The ICE is equipped with a Diesel Oxi-
dation Catalyst (DOC) and a Selective Catalytic Reduction
(SCR) system for exhaust gas aftertreatment. The ICE drives
two hydraulic pumps connected to the engine output shaft.
On the other side, a hydraulic pump for cooling fan is also
connected.

2) WORKING HYDRAULIC SYSTEM
A hydraulic pump with ﬁxed displacement driven by the ICE
provides hydraulic oil ﬂow to the valve system. There are
four cylinders in the hydraulic system, namely two steering
cylinders, one tilt cylinder and one lift cylinder. The lift
and tilt cylinders enable a wide range of work with various
attachments. The most typical attachment is a bucket used for
moving gravel, rocks, and other materials, but other attach-
ments such as forklift, timber grapple, snowplow, sweeper
roller and material handling arm are also used for special
purposes [20]. The steering system is a so-called articulated
steering system. The relative yaw angle between the front and
rear part of the vehicle is changed by two hydraulic cylinders,
allowing the vehicle to be signiﬁcantly more maneuverable
than a vehicle with coordinated steering [21], [22]. The steer-
ing wheel column is connected to the orbitrol, which supplies
oil proportional to the amount of steering wheel rotation to the
steering cylinders in the desired direction. The priority valve
supplies the required oil to the steering cylinders ﬁrst, giving
priority to steering for safety reasons. The remaining oil is
supplied to the open center control valve, where the direction
and ﬂow rate are controlled by the spools.

3) PROPULSION SYSTEM
A hydraulic pump with variable displacement driven by the
ICE forms a hydrostatic transmission (HST) together with a
variable displacement hydraulic motor. All four wheels are
mechanically connected to the output shaft of the hydraulic
motor, enabling all-wheel drive functionality. There is a
hydraulically actuated two-speed transmission between the
HST output shaft and the cardan shaft. With the second gear,
high-speed driving up to 36 km/h is possible.

sections.heading: B. MISSION CYCLES
sections.content:
Wheel loaders cover a wide range of work, and their appli-
cations are versatile. Among others, the most common and
widely studied [23], [24], [25] wheel loader cycle is a loading
cycle, also called a V-cycle because of the shape of the
vehicle movement. Fig. 2 presents a schematic top view
of the V-cycle, while the top two subplots in Fig. 3 show
the measured vehicle speed and cylinder stroke during the
V-cycle. In this cycle, a wheel loader loads materials such as
soil, gravel and sand into a load receiver, which is typically
a truck placed next to a pile of material. The V-cycle can be
divided into four parts. In phase A, the wheel loader moves
forward to a pile of material and ﬁlls the bucket with material.
In phase B, the vehicle drives backwards and returns to the
starting point. In this phase, the bucket’s position remains

VOLUME 14, 2026
3

almost unchanged. In phase C, the vehicle steers slightly
and moves forward towards the load receiver. While driving
forward, the bucket is raised by extending the lift cylinder.
After stopping the vehicle in front of the load receiver, the tilt
cylinder is extended to empty the bucket. Finally, in phase
D, the vehicle reverses and returns to the starting point.
The bucket is lowered by contracting the lift cylinder while
driving backwards. The series of phase A to D is repeated
several times until the load receiver is full of material.

The bottom two subplots in Fig. 3 compare the requested
hydraulic ﬂow rate with the actual supply from the hydraulic
pump. There is a large gap between the supplied ﬂow rate
and the requested ﬂow rate, especially during phase A and
phase B, as marked by red arrows in Fig. 3.
In these phases, the bucket is moved only slightly, resulting
in a low requested ﬂow rate. However, since the hydraulic
pump is connected to the same ICE output shaft as the HST,
it is driven at high speeds when the operator presses the accel-
erator pedal to drive the vehicle. As a result, the hydraulic
pump generates an unnecessarily large amount of oil ﬂow
within the hydraulic system, which returns to the tank without
doing useful hydraulic work. The key to reducing hydraulic
losses from the operational perspective is, therefore, to keep
the pump speed as close as possible to the speed required for
the requested hydraulic ﬂow rate.
Another mission cycle considered in this paper is a combi-
nation of the V-cycle with short driving, as shown in Fig. 4.
This combined cycle serves as a more realistic mission cycle
in a quarry. After ﬁve repetitions of the V-cycle (marked as
1 in Fig. 4), the wheel loader transports material to another
location to increase productivity instead of simply waiting for
another truck to arrive at the loading area. First, the bucket
is loaded (2 in Fig. 4), and then the vehicle drives with a
full bucket (3 in Fig. 4). After transportation, the bucket
is emptied (4 in Fig. 4), and then the vehicle drives the
same route with an empty bucket (5 in Fig. 4) to return to

Y. Kakichi et al.: Real-Time Capable Optimal Energy Management Strategy for a Hybrid Wheel Loader

the loading area. The driving segments are divided into two
distinct parts: a downhill segment with lower drive power
requirements (Drive A) and an uphill segment with higher
drive power requirements (Drive B).

sections.heading: C. PARALLEL-SERIES HYBRID SYSTEM
sections.content:
The powertrain of the baseline wheel loader shown in Fig. 1
has been converted to a parallel-series hybrid system. Fig. 5
shows the schematic of the developed parallel-series hybrid
system for a wheel loader.

The parallel-series hybrid combines aspects of both par-

allel and series topologies. In this conﬁguration, the ICE is
not directly connected to the drivetrain, allowing independent
control of the ICE regardless of the drivetrain speed. The
hydraulic pump is driven by the P2 parallel hybrid system
consisting of an electric machine (P2 EM) and a downsized
ICE. Pure electric operation is possible with the clutch located
between the P2 EM and the ICE.

The hydraulic drivetrain has been electriﬁed with two elec-

tric machines, integrated into each axle. In general, hydraulic
motors have higher torque density compared to electric
motors [26]. A reduction transmission is integrated into each
electric drive unit (EDU) to fulﬁll the maximum vehicle
speed target and the high torque demand at low vehicle
speeds. Details and technical data of the hybrid system are
summarized in Table 1.

sections.heading: D. OPERATOR INTERFACE AND OPERATING STRATEGIES
sections.content:
FOR PARALLEL-SERIES HYBRID SYSTEM
In the conventional wheel loader, the operator presses the
accelerator pedal to regulate the ICE speed to get the desired
hydraulic ﬂow rate from the pump or to get the desired
propulsion torque. This brings with it several drawbacks, and
the operator interface and operating strategies for the hybrid
wheel loader must be designed to overcome them. These are:

1) Low efﬁciency in the working hydraulic system: Since

the hydraulic pump is coupled with the drivetrain via
ICE, the pump runs at high speeds e.g. during vehicle
acceleration even though the hydraulic oil required for
steering is quite low, causing large losses due to excess
ﬂow.

2) High operator workload: As the ICE drives both work-

ing hydraulic pumps, the accelerator pedal position
inﬂuences the pump ﬂow rate and the propulsion
torque. This means that the values controlled by the
operator – cylinder speed and vehicle acceleration –
must be adjusted via additional inputs, namely the joy-
stick and brake pedal.

the parallel-series hybrid wheel loader. Unlike conventional
wheel loaders, all operator inputs are forwarded to the Hybrid
Control Unit (HCU), which determines the target pump speed
and propulsion torque.

Since the propulsion system is decoupled from the working

hydraulic system, the accelerator pedal position is solely used
to determine the propulsion torque. The electriﬁed propulsion
system also offers the possibility of recuperating the kinetic
energy of the vehicle, which in conventional vehicles would
be lost as heat through mechanical brakes, through regenera-
tive braking. By calibrating the target propulsion to a negative
value at a low pedal position, the operator can decelerate
the vehicle by releasing the accelerator pedal. In addition
to efﬁciency beneﬁts, this operating strategy facilitates one-

sections.heading: V. SIMULATIVE INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
In this section, the DP-PMP-based control strategy is com-
pared with the rule-based control strategy through simula-
tions of two different driving cycles. The ﬁrst driving cycle is
a V-cycle repeated ten times. The prediction horizon encom-
passes one loading cycle, which consists of four phases.

The second driving cycle is the combined cycle introduced

in Section II. This cycle includes ﬁve repetitions of the
V-cycle, followed by a bucket loading phase, driving with a
loaded bucket, a bucket emptying phase, and driving with an
empty bucket. It is assumed that all future scenarios, along
with the power/ﬂow demands of the ﬁrst loading cycle and
the ﬁrst two drive states, are known a priori. The power/ﬂow
demand for each state in the prediction horizon is overwritten
once that state is completed.

The rule-based control strategy adopted in this paper shifts

the ICE torque to more fuel-efﬁcient operating points while
maintaining the battery SOC close to the target value [32].
The rule-based ICE start-stop control uses the total vehicle
power demand to switch off the ICE, with a calibratable turn-
off delay time. The turn-off power threshold and turn-off

Y. Kakichi et al.: Real-Time Capable Optimal Energy Management Strategy for a Hybrid Wheel Loader

delay time are calibrated so that the ICE remains on during
the V-cycle, thereby avoiding frequent ICE start-stop events
during highly transient operations.

sections.heading: A. V-CYCLE
sections.content:
Since the investigated cycle consists of repeated, nearly

identical loading cycles, the battery SOC in the rule-based
strategy does not deviate signiﬁcantly from the target value.
Consequently, the battery SOC remains close to the target
value at the end of each loading cycle.

Compared to the rule-based strategy, which is calibrated

to keep the ICE on during the V-cycle, the DP-PMP-based
strategy uses the ICE more effectively by combining electric
operation, while keeping the battery SOC around the tar-
get value through cycle-to-cycle updates of the equivalence
factor. By discharging the battery in the electric mode, the
required charge power to balance the battery SOC increases,
resulting in a shift of the ICE torque to lower BSFC areas in
hybrid mode.

rected by the battery SOC deviation from the target value at
the end of the cycle. Under the tested conditions, DP-PMP

The DP-PMP-based control strategy was implemented in the

results are for the ﬁrst optimization; hence the prediction

loading, drive, bucket emptying, and drive). Upon detecting
the start of the ﬁrst V-cycle at 169.1 second, the optimization

The calculation time for the ﬁve iterations is 2.2 seconds on

sections.heading: B. COMPARISON OF SYSTEM EFFICIENCY
sections.content:
Table 7 summarizes the test results for the V-cycle. The
V-cycle, consisting of 8 loading cycles, was measured four
times with the rule-based control strategy and three times
with the DP-PMP-based strategy. Control parameters were
not changed during the test; only the control strategy was
switched.
Even though the same operator performed the V-cycle,
the amount of work done by the wheel loader varies from
measurement to measurement, as indicated in the second
column from the right in Table 7. This variability arises from
the fact that the wheel loader is equipped with a bucket and
the loading phase in particular is a challenge to reproduce
consistently, even for an experienced operator. Additionally,
the V-shaped wheel loader trace may not be identical in
every cycle, which further increases variability. This makes it
difﬁcult to compare fuel consumption between different mea-
surements and to evaluate fuel consumption beneﬁts based
solely on SOC-corrected fuel consumption, which is subject
to considerable variations.
One way to evaluate fuel efﬁciency is by comparing the
BSFC of the ICE, as both control strategies aim to operate
the ICE in higher efﬁciency areas. The BSFC with DP-PMP is
lower than that with the rule-based strategy overall. In partic-
ular, the average BSFC with DP-PMP is 216.8 g/kWh, which

is 0.7% lower compared to the average BSFC with the rule-
based strategy of 218.4 g/kWh, as shown in the left side of
Fig. 20. This result conﬁrms that DP-PMP uses the ICE more
effectively by using electric mode.
Similar to the V-cycle, the results for the combined cycle
in Table 8 show that the SOC corrected fuel consumption
varies signiﬁcantly from measurement to measurement due
to different amounts of work performed by the vehicle, even
when the same control strategy was engaged. However, the
average BSFC with DP-PMP of 216.3 g/kWh is lower than
that of the rule-based strategy of 219.2 g/kWh, a reduction of
1.3% as shown in the right side of Fig. 20.

Of particular note is that the third measurement with the
rule-based strategy (RB 3) shows a signiﬁcantly higher BSFC
compared to the other two measurements with the same
strategy. In this measurement, the battery SOC decreased
due to an initial SOC that was higher than the target value.
In this scenario, the controller had to discharge the battery.
The rule-based controller discharges the battery by reducing
the ICE torque during the V-cycle in order to bring the battery
SOC to the target value. Consequently, the ICE operates in
lower-efﬁciency areas.
On the other hand, the optimization-based control strategy
can manage the charge-depleting scenarios, by efﬁciently

surement with DP-PMP (DP-PMP 2) shows that the BSFC
remains low in such scenarios. This suggests that the
optimization-based strategy offers greater fuel consumption

those where external battery charging is possible. To fully
exploit the potential of the proposed control strategy in charge
depleting scenarios, optimization of the SOC trajectory
through better task scheduling using sophisticated systems
such as a ﬂeet management system would be required.

sections.heading: VII. CONCLUSION
sections.content:
This paper has presented a novel real-time capable energy
management strategy based on the DP-PMP algorithm for
a hybrid wheel loader. To enable real-time implementation,
wheel loader mission cycles were divided into small seg-
ments, and a future power demand prediction algorithm based
on the repetitiveness of the mission cycles was introduced.
Additionally, the timing of the ICE start-stop control decision
was changed from the conventional time-based approach to
machine state changes in order to further reduce the compu-
tational effort and to avoid unnecessary ICE start-stop events.

15

The developed energy management algorithm was tested

in a simulation environment, and the simulation results
conﬁrmed that the proposed strategy can reduce fuel con-
sumption by 3.3% in the V-cycle and 4.0% in the combined
cycle.

A detailed analysis of the powertrain energy ﬂow has

shown that the optimization-based control strategy reduces
losses in the hydraulic system by reducing the pump speed
in electric mode and uses the ICE more efﬁciently in areas
with lower BSFC. The test results with the demonstrator con-
ﬁrmed that the required time for the optimization calculation
is 2.2 seconds on the MABX II, proving that the proposed
strategy is capable of real-time operation. The test results with
the hybrid wheel loader conﬁrmed that the presented control
strategy can improve the BSFC of the ICE in both the V-cycle
and the combined cycle by using the ICE in areas with higher
efﬁciency. However, due to the varying workloads during
testing, it is difﬁcult to evaluate the overall fuel consumption
beneﬁts.

The proposed approach relies on correct state detection

to trigger optimization based on predicted power demand.
In practical implementation, when state detection conﬁdence
is insufﬁcient or misclassiﬁcation is detected, the controller
intentionally disables the DP–PMP optimization and falls
back to a conservative baseline strategy, such as a rule-
based controller or adaptive ECMS. This fallback mechanism
ensures robust and safe operation under uncertain or unfore-
seen conditions, while preserving the beneﬁts of optimization
when reliable predictions are available.

Future research could focus on analyzing the potential

for reducing raw pollutant emissions through reduced tran-
sient ICE operation, thanks to hybridization. Furthermore, the
integration of emission control into the optimization control
framework to investigate the optimal concept for exhaust
aftertreatment systems is another area for future studies.
In addition, the provision of future scenarios through the
networking of machines and their management as a ﬂeet on
the construction site is another research focus.

Corresponding author: Yuki Kakichi (kakichiyuki.de@gmail.com)
ABSTRACT
Hybrid technologies are considered one of the key solutions for CO2 reduction in large
off-highway machines that operate for long hours in suburban areas with limited access to energy refueling
infrastructure. The effectiveness of CO2 reduction through hybridization largely depends on the hybrid
powertrain architecture and its operating strategies. This paper uses a parallel-series hybrid wheel loader
as a research platform to investigate and optimize energy management strategies. The parallel-series
hybrid powertrain consists of a pure electric propulsion system and a parallel hybrid working hydraulic
system. In this paper, a real-time capable energy management strategy based on an optimization theory is
presented. This strategy combines Dynamic Programming (DP) and Pontryagin’s Minimum Principle (PMP)
to optimize both engine start-stop sequence and torque split between the engine and the electric machine,
while balancing the disadvantages of each control theory. To enable real-time implementation of the proposed
control strategy, short-term vehicle power demand is predicted using a state detection algorithm developed
to account for the repetitive nature of the duty cycles of a wheel loader. Simulation results indicate that
fuel consumption can be reduced by 4.0% compared to a rule-based strategy in a typical loading cycle. Test
results with a prototype hybrid wheel loader conﬁrm that the proposed control strategy operates in real-time
and improves system efﬁciency. In particular, the average engine brake fuel consumption (BSFC) improved
by 0.7% in the loading cycle and by 1.3% in a more realistic mission cycle that combines the loading cycle
with driving.

Pontryagin’s minimum principle (PMP), optimal control.

also on its energy management strategies. An overview and

classiﬁcation of energy management strategies developed for
off-highway machines can be found in [6] and [7]. A primary
distinction is made between rule-based and optimization-
based control strategies.
In rule-based control strategies, control decisions are made
based on predeﬁned rules derived from prior knowledge of
the system, operating conditions, and empirical experience.
These strategies are often preferred for real-world vehicle
implementation because of their low computational effort.
For this reason, existing hybrid construction machines pri-
marily adopt rule-based strategies [6], and extensive research
has been conducted in this area. In [8], a rule-based strategy
was developed for an excavator equipped with a parallel
hybrid system for the hydraulic pump and an electric swing
motor. This strategy adjusts the motor-generator power based
on the required pump power. Similarly, in [9], various rule-
based control strategies were designed for a parallel hybrid
wheel loader. These strategies were evaluated in simulations
in terms of fuel efﬁciency and achieved a 3–13% reduction in
fuel consumption compared to a conventional wheel loader.
Rule-based control strategies have also been validated in
real-world operations. In [10], a prototype hybrid excavator
with a parallel hybrid system for the pump and an electric
swing motor was developed. A rule-based control strategy
was implemented and tested in this prototype excavator.
Rule-based strategies are simple and have a low compu-
tational effort. However, they are typically optimized for a
speciﬁc mission cycle and do not guarantee the same level of
performance in real-world cycles.
In contrast, optimization-based strategies introduce control
objectives by deﬁning cost functions to be optimized and
thus providing proof of optimality. Dynamic Programming
(DP) [11] is one of the most widely used techniques for
global optimization. However, DP requires prior knowledge
of the entire cycle, and its high computational burden makes
real-time energy management highly challenging. In [12],
a rule-based control strategy for a hybrid excavator was
developed by analyzing the results of a DP-based control
strategy. Furthermore, DP is also used as a benchmark
strategy [13], [14].
Control strategies based on Pontryagin’s Minimum Princi-
ple (PMP) are strong candidates for real-time capable control
strategies. The application of the Equivalent Consump-
tion Minimization Strategy (ECMS) to off-highway hybrid
machines has been widely documented in the literature [13],
[14], [15]. In [13], an ECMS-based energy management strat-
egy was implemented in a hybrid excavator equipped with an
electric swing motor. Test results with the real vehicle demon-
strated approximately 30% reduction in fuel consumption
compared to a conventional excavator. PMP-based strategies
require lower computational effort but cannot handle discrete
states, such as mode transitions and gear shifts, within their
control framework. To address this limitation, the authors
of [16] combined DP and PMP to derive the optimal start-
stop sequence of the internal combustion engine (ICE) for
plug-in electric vehicles. Their simulations conﬁrmed that the
DP-PMP algorithm yields near-optimal performance. Other
studies [17], [18], [19] extended this approach to optimize
both ICE start-stop and gear shifting for on-highway hybrid
vehicles. However, to the best of the authors’ knowledge,
DP-PMP-based energy management strategies have not yet
been validated through real-world testing. Furthermore, their
application is limited to on-highway vehicles so far. In this
paper, we propose a DP-PMP-based control algorithm as a
real-time energy management strategy for a hybrid wheel
loader. The main contributions of this paper are as follows:
• We adapt the DP-PMP approach to off-highway hybrid
powertrains and formulate an energy management
algorithm.
• We present the control architecture, including support
functions, to ensure real-time implementation of the
developed algorithm.
• We evaluate control performance in terms of fuel con-
sumption in both simulation and real-world testing.
Additionally, we assess the real-time capability of the
controller.
The rest of this paper is structured as follows: Section II
presents the developed hybrid powertrain and the investigated
mission cycles. Section III describes the modeling of key
powertrain components for the implementation of an optimal
control strategy. Section IV details the adopted optimal con-
trol algorithm, the controller design, and its implementation
in the prototype hybrid wheel loader. The developed con-
trol algorithm is evaluated through simulations in Section V
and validated via real-world testing in Section VI. Finally,
Section VII concludes the paper.

II. PARALLEL-SERIES HYBRID SYSTEM
A. CONVENTIONAL POWERTRAIN
A conventional 7-ton class wheel loader depicted in Fig. 1
is used as a baseline for research. The powertrain of the
conventional wheel loader consists of three sub-systems:
1) POWER SOURCE
The baseline wheel loader is powered by a 3.6 L, 4-cylinder
Diesel internal combustion engine (ICE) with a maximum
Y. Kakichi et al.: Real-Time Capable Optimal Energy Management Strategy for a Hybrid Wheel Loader
2
VOLUME 14, 2026
power of 74.4 kW. The ICE is equipped with a Diesel Oxi-
dation Catalyst (DOC) and a Selective Catalytic Reduction
(SCR) system for exhaust gas aftertreatment. The ICE drives
two hydraulic pumps connected to the engine output shaft.
On the other side, a hydraulic pump for cooling fan is also
connected.
2) WORKING HYDRAULIC SYSTEM
A hydraulic pump with ﬁxed displacement driven by the ICE
provides hydraulic oil ﬂow to the valve system. There are
four cylinders in the hydraulic system, namely two steering
cylinders, one tilt cylinder and one lift cylinder. The lift
and tilt cylinders enable a wide range of work with various
attachments. The most typical attachment is a bucket used for
moving gravel, rocks, and other materials, but other attach-
ments such as forklift, timber grapple, snowplow, sweeper
roller and material handling arm are also used for special
purposes [20]. The steering system is a so-called articulated
steering system. The relative yaw angle between the front and
rear part of the vehicle is changed by two hydraulic cylinders,
allowing the vehicle to be signiﬁcantly more maneuverable
than a vehicle with coordinated steering [21], [22]. The steer-
ing wheel column is connected to the orbitrol, which supplies
oil proportional to the amount of steering wheel rotation to the
steering cylinders in the desired direction. The priority valve
supplies the required oil to the steering cylinders ﬁrst, giving
priority to steering for safety reasons. The remaining oil is
supplied to the open center control valve, where the direction
and ﬂow rate are controlled by the spools.
3) PROPULSION SYSTEM
A hydraulic pump with variable displacement driven by the
ICE forms a hydrostatic transmission (HST) together with a
variable displacement hydraulic motor. All four wheels are
mechanically connected to the output shaft of the hydraulic
motor, enabling all-wheel drive functionality. There is a
hydraulically actuated two-speed transmission between the
HST output shaft and the cardan shaft. With the second gear,
high-speed driving up to 36 km/h is possible.
B. MISSION CYCLES
Wheel loaders cover a wide range of work, and their appli-
cations are versatile. Among others, the most common and
widely studied [23], [24], [25] wheel loader cycle is a loading
cycle, also called a V-cycle because of the shape of the
vehicle movement. Fig. 2 presents a schematic top view
of the V-cycle, while the top two subplots in Fig. 3 show
the measured vehicle speed and cylinder stroke during the
V-cycle. In this cycle, a wheel loader loads materials such as
soil, gravel and sand into a load receiver, which is typically
a truck placed next to a pile of material. The V-cycle can be
divided into four parts. In phase A, the wheel loader moves
forward to a pile of material and ﬁlls the bucket with material.
In phase B, the vehicle drives backwards and returns to the
starting point. In this phase, the bucket’s position remains
almost unchanged. In phase C, the vehicle steers slightly
and moves forward towards the load receiver. While driving
forward, the bucket is raised by extending the lift cylinder.
After stopping the vehicle in front of the load receiver, the tilt
cylinder is extended to empty the bucket. Finally, in phase
D, the vehicle reverses and returns to the starting point.
The bucket is lowered by contracting the lift cylinder while
driving backwards. The series of phase A to D is repeated
several times until the load receiver is full of material.
FIGURE 2. Schematic top view of the V-cycle.
The bottom two subplots in Fig. 3 compare the requested
hydraulic ﬂow rate with the actual supply from the hydraulic
pump. There is a large gap between the supplied ﬂow rate
and the requested ﬂow rate, especially during phase A and
phase B, as marked by red arrows in Fig. 3.
In these phases, the bucket is moved only slightly, resulting
in a low requested ﬂow rate. However, since the hydraulic
pump is connected to the same ICE output shaft as the HST,
it is driven at high speeds when the operator presses the accel-
erator pedal to drive the vehicle. As a result, the hydraulic
pump generates an unnecessarily large amount of oil ﬂow
within the hydraulic system, which returns to the tank without
doing useful hydraulic work. The key to reducing hydraulic
losses from the operational perspective is, therefore, to keep
the pump speed as close as possible to the speed required for
the requested hydraulic ﬂow rate.
Another mission cycle considered in this paper is a combi-
nation of the V-cycle with short driving, as shown in Fig. 4.
This combined cycle serves as a more realistic mission cycle
in a quarry. After ﬁve repetitions of the V-cycle (marked as
1 in Fig. 4), the wheel loader transports material to another

C. PARALLEL-SERIES HYBRID SYSTEM
The powertrain of the baseline wheel loader shown in Fig. 1
has been converted to a parallel-series hybrid system. Fig. 5
shows the schematic of the developed parallel-series hybrid
system for a wheel loader.
The parallel-series hybrid combines aspects of both par-
allel and series topologies. In this conﬁguration, the ICE is
not directly connected to the drivetrain, allowing independent
control of the ICE regardless of the drivetrain speed. The
hydraulic pump is driven by the P2 parallel hybrid system
consisting of an electric machine (P2 EM) and a downsized
ICE. Pure electric operation is possible with the clutch located
between the P2 EM and the ICE.
The hydraulic drivetrain has been electriﬁed with two elec-
tric machines, integrated into each axle. In general, hydraulic
motors have higher torque density compared to electric
motors [26]. A reduction transmission is integrated into each
electric drive unit (EDU) to fulﬁll the maximum vehicle
speed target and the high torque demand at low vehicle
speeds. Details and technical data of the hybrid system are

D. OPERATOR INTERFACE AND OPERATING STRATEGIES
FOR PARALLEL-SERIES HYBRID SYSTEM
In the conventional wheel loader, the operator presses the
accelerator pedal to regulate the ICE speed to get the desired
hydraulic ﬂow rate from the pump or to get the desired
propulsion torque. This brings with it several drawbacks, and
the operator interface and operating strategies for the hybrid
wheel loader must be designed to overcome them. These are:
1) Low efﬁciency in the working hydraulic system: Since
the hydraulic pump is coupled with the drivetrain via
ICE, the pump runs at high speeds e.g. during vehicle
acceleration even though the hydraulic oil required for
steering is quite low, causing large losses due to excess
ﬂow.
2) High operator workload: As the ICE drives both work-
ing hydraulic pumps, the accelerator pedal position
inﬂuences the pump ﬂow rate and the propulsion
torque. This means that the values controlled by the
operator – cylinder speed and vehicle acceleration –
must be adjusted via additional inputs, namely the joy-
stick and brake pedal.
Fig. 7. shows the new operator interface developed for
the parallel-series hybrid wheel loader. Unlike conventional
wheel loaders, all operator inputs are forwarded to the Hybrid
Control Unit (HCU), which determines the target pump speed
and propulsion torque.
Since the propulsion system is decoupled from the working
hydraulic system, the accelerator pedal position is solely used
to determine the propulsion torque. The electriﬁed propulsion
system also offers the possibility of recuperating the kinetic
energy of the vehicle, which in conventional vehicles would
be lost as heat through mechanical brakes, through regenera-
tive braking. By calibrating the target propulsion to a negative
value at a low pedal position, the operator can decelerate
the vehicle by releasing the accelerator pedal. In addition
to efﬁciency beneﬁts, this operating strategy facilitates one-

VII. CONCLUSION
This paper has presented a novel real-time capable energy
management strategy based on the DP-PMP algorithm for
a hybrid wheel loader. To enable real-time implementation,
wheel loader mission cycles were divided into small seg-
ments, and a future power demand prediction algorithm based
on the repetitiveness of the mission cycles was introduced.
Additionally, the timing of the ICE start-stop control decision
was changed from the conventional time-based approach to
machine state changes in order to further reduce the compu-
tational effort and to avoid unnecessary ICE start-stop events.
The developed energy management algorithm was tested
in a simulation environment, and the simulation results
conﬁrmed that the proposed strategy can reduce fuel con-
sumption by 3.3% in the V-cycle and 4.0% in the combined
cycle.
A detailed analysis of the powertrain energy ﬂow has
shown that the optimization-based control strategy reduces
losses in the hydraulic system by reducing the pump speed
in electric mode and uses the ICE more efﬁciently in areas
with lower BSFC. The test results with the demonstrator con-
ﬁrmed that the required time for the optimization calculation
is 2.2 seconds on the MABX II, proving that the proposed
strategy is capable of real-time operation. The test results with
the hybrid wheel loader conﬁrmed that the presented control
strategy can improve the BSFC of the ICE in both the V-cycle
and the combined cycle by using the ICE in areas with higher
efﬁciency. However, due to the varying workloads during
testing, it is difﬁcult to evaluate the overall fuel consumption
beneﬁts.
The proposed approach relies on correct state detection
to trigger optimization based on predicted power demand.
In practical implementation, when state detection conﬁdence
is insufﬁcient or misclassiﬁcation is detected, the controller
intentionally disables the DP–PMP optimization and falls
back to a conservative baseline strategy, such as a rule-
based controller or adaptive ECMS. This fallback mechanism
ensures robust and safe operation under uncertain or unfore-
seen conditions, while preserving the beneﬁts of optimization
when reliable predictions are available.
Future research could focus on analyzing the potential
for reducing raw pollutant emissions through reduced tran-
sient ICE operation, thanks to hybridization. Furthermore, the
integration of emission control into the optimization control
framework to investigate the optimal concept for exhaust
aftertreatment systems is another area for future studies.
In addition, the provision of future scenarios through the
networking of machines and their management as a ﬂeet on
the construction site is another research focus.

ABSTRACT
Hybrid technologies are considered one of the key solutions for CO2 reduction in large
off-highway machines that operate for long hours in suburban areas with limited access to energy refueling
infrastructure. The effectiveness of CO2 reduction through hybridization largely depends on the hybrid
powertrain architecture and its operating strategies. This paper uses a parallel-series hybrid wheel loader
as a research platform to investigate and optimize energy management strategies. The parallel-series
hybrid powertrain consists of a pure electric propulsion system and a parallel hybrid working hydraulic
system. In this paper, a real-time capable energy management strategy based on an optimization theory is
presented. This strategy combines Dynamic Programming (DP) and Pontryagin’s Minimum Principle (PMP)
to optimize both engine start-stop sequence and torque split between the engine and the electric machine,
while balancing the disadvantages of each control theory. To enable real-time implementation of the proposed
control strategy, short-term vehicle power demand is predicted using a state detection algorithm developed
to account for the repetitive nature of the duty cycles of a wheel loader. Simulation results indicate that
fuel consumption can be reduced by 4.0% compared to a rule-based strategy in a typical loading cycle. Test
results with a prototype hybrid wheel loader conﬁrm that the proposed control strategy operates in real-time
and improves system efﬁciency. In particular, the average engine brake fuel consumption (BSFC) improved
by 0.7% in the loading cycle and by 1.3% in a more realistic mission cycle that combines the loading cycle
with driving.

swing motor was developed. A rule-based control strategy
was implemented and tested in this prototype excavator.
Rule-based strategies are simple and have a low compu-
tational effort. However, they are typically optimized for a
speciﬁc mission cycle and do not guarantee the same level of
performance in real-world cycles.
In contrast, optimization-based strategies introduce control
objectives by deﬁning cost functions to be optimized and
thus providing proof of optimality. Dynamic Programming
(DP) [11] is one of the most widely used techniques for
global optimization. However, DP requires prior knowledge
of the entire cycle, and its high computational burden makes
real-time energy management highly challenging. In [12],
a rule-based control strategy for a hybrid excavator was
developed by analyzing the results of a DP-based control
strategy. Furthermore, DP is also used as a benchmark
strategy [13], [14].
Control strategies based on Pontryagin’s Minimum Princi-
ple (PMP) are strong candidates for real-time capable control
strategies. The application of the Equivalent Consump-
tion Minimization Strategy (ECMS) to off-highway hybrid
machines has been widely documented in the literature [13],
[14], [15]. In [13], an ECMS-based energy management strat-
egy was implemented in a hybrid excavator equipped with an
electric swing motor. Test results with the real vehicle demon-
strated approximately 30% reduction in fuel consumption
compared to a conventional excavator. PMP-based strategies
require lower computational effort but cannot handle discrete
states, such as mode transitions and gear shifts, within their
control framework. To address this limitation, the authors
of [16] combined DP and PMP to derive the optimal start-
stop sequence of the internal combustion engine (ICE) for
plug-in electric vehicles. Their simulations conﬁrmed that the
DP-PMP algorithm yields near-optimal performance. Other
studies [17], [18], [19] extended this approach to optimize
both ICE start-stop and gear shifting for on-highway hybrid
vehicles. However, to the best of the authors’ knowledge,
DP-PMP-based energy management strategies have not yet
been validated through real-world testing. Furthermore, their
application is limited to on-highway vehicles so far. In this
paper, we propose a DP-PMP-based control algorithm as a
real-time energy management strategy for a hybrid wheel
loader. The main contributions of this paper are as follows:
• We adapt the DP-PMP approach to off-highway hybrid
powertrains and formulate an energy management
algorithm.
• We present the control architecture, including support
functions, to ensure real-time implementation of the
developed algorithm.
• We evaluate control performance in terms of fuel con-
sumption in both simulation and real-world testing.
Additionally, we assess the real-time capability of the
controller.

B. MISSION CYCLES
Wheel loaders cover a wide range of work, and their appli-
cations are versatile. Among others, the most common and
widely studied [23], [24], [25] wheel loader cycle is a loading
cycle, also called a V-cycle because of the shape of the
vehicle movement. Fig. 2 presents a schematic top view
of the V-cycle, while the top two subplots in Fig. 3 show
the measured vehicle speed and cylinder stroke during the
V-cycle. In this cycle, a wheel loader loads materials such as
soil, gravel and sand into a load receiver, which is typically
a truck placed next to a pile of material. The V-cycle can be
divided into four parts. In phase A, the wheel loader moves
forward to a pile of material and ﬁlls the bucket with material.
In phase B, the vehicle drives backwards and returns to the
starting point. In this phase, the bucket’s position remains
almost unchanged. In phase C, the vehicle steers slightly
and moves forward towards the load receiver. While driving
forward, the bucket is raised by extending the lift cylinder.
After stopping the vehicle in front of the load receiver, the tilt
cylinder is extended to empty the bucket. Finally, in phase
D, the vehicle reverses and returns to the starting point.
The bucket is lowered by contracting the lift cylinder while
driving backwards. The series of phase A to D is repeated
several times until the load receiver is full of material.

C. PARALLEL-SERIES HYBRID SYSTEM
The powertrain of the baseline wheel loader shown in Fig. 1
has been converted to a parallel-series hybrid system. Fig. 5
shows the schematic of the developed parallel-series hybrid
system for a wheel loader.
The parallel-series hybrid combines aspects of both par-
allel and series topologies. In this conﬁguration, the ICE is
not directly connected to the drivetrain, allowing independent
control of the ICE regardless of the drivetrain speed. The
hydraulic pump is driven by the P2 parallel hybrid system
consisting of an electric machine (P2 EM) and a downsized
ICE. Pure electric operation is possible with the clutch located
between the P2 EM and the ICE.
The hydraulic drivetrain has been electriﬁed with two elec-
tric machines, integrated into each axle. In general, hydraulic
motors have higher torque density compared to electric
motors [26]. A reduction transmission is integrated into each
electric drive unit (EDU) to fulﬁll the maximum vehicle
speed target and the high torque demand at low vehicle

D. OPERATOR INTERFACE AND OPERATING STRATEGIES
FOR PARALLEL-SERIES HYBRID SYSTEM
In the conventional wheel loader, the operator presses the
accelerator pedal to regulate the ICE speed to get the desired
hydraulic ﬂow rate from the pump or to get the desired
propulsion torque. This brings with it several drawbacks, and
the operator interface and operating strategies for the hybrid
wheel loader must be designed to overcome them. These are:
1) Low efﬁciency in the working hydraulic system: Since
the hydraulic pump is coupled with the drivetrain via
ICE, the pump runs at high speeds e.g. during vehicle
acceleration even though the hydraulic oil required for
steering is quite low, causing large losses due to excess
ﬂow.
2) High operator workload: As the ICE drives both work-
ing hydraulic pumps, the accelerator pedal position
inﬂuences the pump ﬂow rate and the propulsion
torque. This means that the values controlled by the
operator – cylinder speed and vehicle acceleration –
must be adjusted via additional inputs, namely the joy-
stick and brake pedal.
Fig. 7. shows the new operator interface developed for
the parallel-series hybrid wheel loader. Unlike conventional
wheel loaders, all operator inputs are forwarded to the Hybrid
Control Unit (HCU), which determines the target pump speed
and propulsion torque.
Since the propulsion system is decoupled from the working
hydraulic system, the accelerator pedal position is solely used
to determine the propulsion torque. The electriﬁed propulsion
system also offers the possibility of recuperating the kinetic
energy of the vehicle, which in conventional vehicles would
be lost as heat through mechanical brakes, through regenera-
tive braking. By calibrating the target propulsion to a negative
value at a low pedal position, the operator can decelerate
the vehicle by releasing the accelerator pedal. In addition
to efﬁciency beneﬁts, this operating strategy facilitates one-

repeated with the updated equivalence factor until the termi-

state for each state and the optimal equivalence factor are
obtained as the output of the calculation.

VII. CONCLUSION
This paper has presented a novel real-time capable energy
management strategy based on the DP-PMP algorithm for
a hybrid wheel loader. To enable real-time implementation,
wheel loader mission cycles were divided into small seg-
ments, and a future power demand prediction algorithm based
on the repetitiveness of the mission cycles was introduced.
Additionally, the timing of the ICE start-stop control decision
was changed from the conventional time-based approach to
machine state changes in order to further reduce the compu-
tational effort and to avoid unnecessary ICE start-stop events.
The developed energy management algorithm was tested
in a simulation environment, and the simulation results
conﬁrmed that the proposed strategy can reduce fuel con-
sumption by 3.3% in the V-cycle and 4.0% in the combined
cycle.
A detailed analysis of the powertrain energy ﬂow has
shown that the optimization-based control strategy reduces
losses in the hydraulic system by reducing the pump speed
in electric mode and uses the ICE more efﬁciently in areas
with lower BSFC. The test results with the demonstrator con-
ﬁrmed that the required time for the optimization calculation
is 2.2 seconds on the MABX II, proving that the proposed
strategy is capable of real-time operation. The test results with
the hybrid wheel loader conﬁrmed that the presented control
strategy can improve the BSFC of the ICE in both the V-cycle
and the combined cycle by using the ICE in areas with higher
efﬁciency. However, due to the varying workloads during
testing, it is difﬁcult to evaluate the overall fuel consumption
beneﬁts.
The proposed approach relies on correct state detection
to trigger optimization based on predicted power demand.
In practical implementation, when state detection conﬁdence
is insufﬁcient or misclassiﬁcation is detected, the controller
intentionally disables the DP–PMP optimization and falls
back to a conservative baseline strategy, such as a rule-
based controller or adaptive ECMS. This fallback mechanism
ensures robust and safe operation under uncertain or unfore-
seen conditions, while preserving the beneﬁts of optimization
when reliable predictions are available.
Future research could focus on analyzing the potential
for reducing raw pollutant emissions through reduced tran-
sient ICE operation, thanks to hybridization. Furthermore, the
integration of emission control into the optimization control
framework to investigate the optimal concept for exhaust
aftertreatment systems is another area for future studies.
In addition, the provision of future scenarios through the
networking of machines and their management as a ﬂeet on
the construction site is another research focus.
